title: Putin Frees US Teacher Hubbard as Witkoff Pushes to Resume Three-Way Ukraine Talks
excerpt: Russia released 74-year-old Stephen Hubbard during Steve Witkoff's ninth meeting with Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg, as Washington pressed for direct US-Russia-Ukraine negotiations on a peace framework first shaped in Oslo.
body:
• Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired US schoolteacher held since April 2022, during Steve Witkoff's meeting with Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday.
  • Witkoff urged Putin to resume direct three-way talks among the US, Russia and Ukraine, carrying proposals agreed with Kyiv and European partners in Oslo a day earlier.
  • It was Witkoff's ninth in-person meeting with Putin; Moscow has not moved on its core demands for the Donbas region and a bar on Ukrainian NATO membership.
  • A US official said the Oslo talks made meaningful progress on security guarantees, a post-war economic plan and a wider European security framework.

President Vladimir Putin hosted US special envoy Steve Witkoff at the Constantine Palace in St Petersburg on Wednesday, in a three-hour meeting that opened with a goodwill gesture: Russia freed Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired American schoolteacher who had been held since 2022. According to Reuters, Putin told Witkoff that Hubbard was already at the airport waiting to fly back to the United States with him.

Witkoff flew in on Wednesday morning, a day after what a US official called constructive talks in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and the leaders of Finland and Norway, alongside European and NATO representatives. He arrived in St Petersburg, in Reuters' account, armed with ideas from Oslo and aiming to create a pathway toward direct trilateral and broader multilateral negotiations. CNN reported that Witkoff implored Putin to consider resuming trilateral Russia-US-Ukraine talks at which technical issues could be discussed, and that the two sides agreed talks would continue toward planned technical-level discussions involving all three countries.

A prisoner release as the opening move

Hubbard was first detained in April 2022 and later sentenced to six years and ten months on mercenary charges that he denies and that his family and US-based lawyer question. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he had raised the idea of freeing Hubbard with Putin directly. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin freed Hubbard at Trump's request and had also taken the American's poor health into account. Hubbard's son, Joseph Coleman, told Reuters he spoke briefly by phone with his father before he boarded the plane in Russia, saying he seemed light in his step, with a sense of happiness in his voice.

"I think there's some degree of momentum, and I hope that this today can be another step forward in the peace process."

— Steve Witkoff, US Special Envoy

Witkoff thanked Putin for the release and called the talks constructive. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the Oslo meeting had been positive and that Witkoff would share its results with the Russian side: armed with those ideas, he could go to St Petersburg and see whether progress was possible.

What Oslo put on the table

A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Ukraine brought new ideas and proposals to Oslo that made meaningful progress toward a coordinated approach to engaging Russia. The talks covered key elements of a comprehensive peace framework, including long-term security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic and prosperity plan, and a broader European security architecture designed to create lasting stability. Zelenskiy said Ukraine also wants trilateral negotiations involving Trump, Putin and himself, though he balked at any format that discussed Ukraine without Ukraine at the table.

Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy and his main point man for potential economic deals with the US, attended the St Petersburg meeting, according to Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov. CNN reported that Putin expressed interest in restoring economic cooperation with the United States and in a possible meeting with China to discuss Ukraine, and that Dmitriev said afterwards there was no question US-Russian economic cooperation would continue.

The gaps that remain

None of Wednesday's warmth changed the stated positions. Putin has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims, which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and no NATO membership for Kyiv; Ukraine and its allies restated their red lines in Oslo, including future security guarantees and a rejection of demands to give up territory. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov struck a cooler tone on Tuesday, saying Moscow would not make political concessions and did not expect a miracle.

The meeting also came amid friction inside the Western camp. US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month, and Ukraine has complained of disruption to intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelenskiy said the Oslo meeting reached agreement to resolve those issues. Trump, for his part, kept pressure on Kyiv on the eve of the talks, saying Zelenskiy would have to want to make a deal because his people would not stand for the war much longer.

What happens next

The immediate test is whether the planned technical-level discussions among the US, Russia and Ukraine are scheduled and staffed. The latest talks came more than two years after Trump promised during his election campaign to end the war within 24 hours; Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two is now in its fifth year. For now, Washington has a released prisoner, a channel that both sides describe as constructive, and no public evidence that Moscow's terms have softened.
